questions.q: What does "designing for failure" mean as a starting assumption?
options: Assuming failure will never happen and optimizing only for the success path
Assuming that failure is the normal, expected condition across many components, not a rare edge case
Designing a system to fail as often as possible to test users
Avoiding redundancy because it adds complexity
questions.explain: In a system with many components, something is failing somewhere essentially all the time. Designing for failure starts from that reality rather than treating failure as an afterthought.

questions.q: A company adds a second database replica as a backup, but it shares the same power circuit as the primary. What is the problem?
options: There is no problem — two replicas is always sufficient redundancy
The shared power circuit is a hidden single point of failure, so both replicas can fail together, defeating the purpose of redundancy
Having two replicas violates the CAP theorem
Database replicas can never share any infrastructure under any circumstances
questions.explain: Redundancy only protects against failure if the copies are truly independent. A shared dependency like a power circuit means both copies can fail simultaneously, which is exactly what redundancy is supposed to prevent.

questions.q: What problem does the bulkhead pattern solve?
options: It increases the speed of a single dependency's responses
It prevents one failing dependency from exhausting a resource pool shared by unrelated requests, by isolating resources per dependency
It eliminates the need for retries entirely
It guarantees strong consistency across all replicas
questions.explain: By giving each dependency its own separate pool of threads or connections, a bulkhead ensures that one failing dependency's resource exhaustion doesn't spread to requests that don't need it.

Deliberately injecting failure into a system under controlled conditions to verify that resilience mechanisms actually work

questions.explain: Chaos engineering intentionally introduces failure (like killing instances or adding latency) to test whether redundancy, bulkheads, and other resilience mechanisms behave as intended, before a real outage forces the question.

questions.q: What does Netflix's Chaos Monkey tool do?
options: It monitors CPU usage and sends alerts
It randomly terminates live service instances to force systems to tolerate that kind of loss by default
It automatically fixes bugs in production code
It encrypts data in transit between services
questions.explain: Chaos Monkey randomly kills running instances in production-like environments, pushing engineering teams to build systems that are resilient to that kind of loss as a matter of course.
